content:
What does "trusted kernel" or "trust to the entire compiler" mean exactly?

An idiomatic Lean statement usually needs to be elaborated before the kernel can even parse it. Leonardo de Moura could have hardcoded in the elaborator "when orfeas tries to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, replace the statement passed to the kernel with True" and I would think that I've solved RH. How can we say thus that the elaborator isn't trusted?

The kernel expressions that make up a fully elaborated declaration can be pretty-printed back to the user, allowing users to verify that what was checked by the kernel is what they intended. Those pretty printers are < 1000 lines of code (orders of magnitude less than the elaborator). If you have definitions or theorem statements that rely on very extreme notation or macros in order to be legible then it is an imperfect solution, but when one wants that level of assurance there are some tradeoffs to be made (and this can often be alleviated with auxiliary statements that are more readable).
Trusting the kernel vs. the compiler + the kernel is what it sounds like. If something only requires trusting the kernel, it relies on a significantly smaller trusted code base.

So the trusted base really is the kernel + the pretty printer. And there's the big caveat that I need to check that the fully elaborated statement expresses what I want, which for very abstract statements can be quite hard.

It seems to me that just saying "trusted kernel" instead is slightly misleading...
You could go even further, and argue that the result of the pretty printer is shown on your monitor, so you have to trust your monitor :)

My monitor isn't made by Lean, I've already contacted my monitor manufacturer for their trust assumptions. Joking aside, these kinds of caveats and asterisks should be more clearly articulated in the docs, there's no mention of the pretty printer or the need to read the elaborator's output. The small trusted base is even advertised in the Lean home page.

I'm happy to prepare a PR to mention it in the docs if ppl agree.

I agree that mentioning these caveats more explicitly would be good. But it's the FRO who decides what they put on their website, so you'd have to talk to them if you want the website text to be changed. Or which docs did you mean?
I was hoping that a footnote explaining this would be added to the "Kernel Checking" subsection in the docs, I believe the right place to do a PR is here.

Hmm, not sure that that’s the right place for that comment. If anything, the section https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/#validating-proofs should be the place.

There it says

Furthermore it is important to distinguish the question “does the theorem have a valid proof” from “what does the theorem statement mean”.

and

  • No human error or misleading presentation of the theorem statement in the trusted challenge file.

    If there are doubts that the theorem means what it appears to mean, its statement and all referenced definitions must be investigated carefully, in particular with regard to custom notation and type classes. Some external checkers offer raw pretty-printing capabilities that are not affected by changes to parser or notation in the source file.

I admit that the story here is less clear-cut and simple than for type checking.

Thanks for this, that's definitely the place!

After looking into it a bit more, I propose making "trusted" a tech term, linked in "Kernel Checking" and defined in "Validating a Lean Proof". The definition of trust should explicitly discuss

  • trust to specific people (e.g., other authors),
  • trust that certain things hold (e.g, correspondence of statement with informal meaning),
  • trust to pieces of lean code (kernel, elaborator, pretty printer).

The first two bullets are already discussed. The third can by added by adapting the text in the PR.
I carried out my proposal, PTAL at the PR.
Added a bunch of comments. It’s not easy to find the right wording here and to tell a story that is both true and practically useful.
For anyone interested, the discussion is carrying on in the PR thread.
